notes.headline: PDD: flat revenue but profit held at RMB31 billion as marketing cuts offset Temu’s shrinking commissions; shares up 11%
notes.takeaway: Revenue was unchanged at RMB108.3 billion, with advertising income up 12% and transaction fees down 12%. Non-GAAP EPS of RMB21.04 per ADS beat the RMB18.8 consensus because sales and marketing spending fell by RMB5 billion, and the shares rose 11% on the day.
results: PDD Holdings reported revenue of RMB108.3 billion (US$16.2 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, the same as a year earlier. Online marketing services — the advertising merchants buy on Pinduoduo — rose 12% to RMB59.8 billion, while transaction services, which include the commissions earned by Temu and Duoduo Maicai, fell 12% to RMB48.5 billion.

Operating expenses fell 12% to RMB31.9 billion, mainly because sales and marketing dropped to RMB25.3 billion from RMB30.3 billion. Operating profit was RMB31.2 billion and non-GAAP net income RMB31.0 billion, almost exactly last year’s RMB31.4 billion. Non-GAAP diluted earnings per ADS were RMB21.04 (US$3.14), against RMB21.08 a year ago and a consensus of about RMB18.8.

Operating cash flow was RMB43.0 billion. Cash and short-term investments reached RMB455.4 billion (US$67.9 billion), with another RMB115.7 billion of mostly time deposits in other non-current assets — together roughly US$85 billion, around two thirds of PDD’s market value.
mgmt: Co-chief executive Jiazhen Zhao said the company continued to deepen its support for merchants and sees significant potential to build on that progress. Co-chief executive Lei Chen said the global business is adapting to an evolving trade and regulatory environment and that PDD remains committed to deepening its supply-chain investments.

Jun Liu, vice-president of finance, repeated that PDD remains in a strategic investment phase and will keep funding merchant-support initiatives with discipline. As usual the company gave no financial guidance and held to its policy of not paying dividends or buying back stock.
view: The headline that revenue did not grow at all would normally be a disaster for a company valued as a growth stock. The market’s 11% rally tells you PDD is no longer valued as one. At around seven times earnings with cash equal to two thirds of its market value, investors are buying a very profitable Chinese marketplace whose overseas arm has stopped being a source of growth and become a source of risk. This quarter showed the profit engine is intact: the domestic advertising business grew 12%, and PDD protected earnings by spending RMB5 billion less on marketing.

The 12% drop in transaction revenue is the Temu story in one number. The end of the US duty-free exemption for small parcels and tighter rules in Europe forced Temu to move from shipping individual parcels from China to a local-warehouse model, which earns less per order and grows more slowly. Management’s careful language about adapting to the trade and regulatory environment is an acknowledgement that the period of hyper-growth abroad is over. The question is whether Temu settles into a smaller but profitable business or becomes a drain.

The persistent discount reflects governance as much as fundamentals. PDD gives no guidance, holds almost no earnings calls of substance, returns nothing to shareholders and sits on a cash pile that grows by RMB30 billion or more each quarter. Until management signals what that cash is for — a buyback, a dividend or a large investment — the shares will trade on the earnings beat of the day rather than on the value of the franchise. Anyone owning PDD should treat any capital-return announcement as the single most important catalyst.
notes.watch: Watch the transaction-services line for signs that Temu’s decline is bottoming, whether the marketing cuts hold without losing share at home to Alibaba and JD, and any change to PDD’s policy of keeping all its cash.
